name: Zoom
tagline: Video meetings and collaboration services for teams and external participants.
description: Zoom is a video communication platform for online meetings, screen sharing, webinars, and related collaboration services. Organizations should evaluate the exact products and plan features they need, including administration, recording, privacy, and integrations.
pros: A familiar meeting workflow can make it easier to host external participants and share screens.
Meeting, webinar, room, and phone options may support organizations with several communication needs.
Host controls and integration options should be evaluated against the organization's identity and scheduling setup.
cons: Advanced events, room, phone, recording, or administration capabilities may require separate products or plan upgrades.
Organizations need clear policies for recording access, retention, and sharing.
Teams already standardized on another collaboration suite should compare integration and administration before switching.

features.name: HD Video Conferencing
features.description: Up to 1080p video with adaptive bitrate streaming, screen sharing, virtual backgrounds, and touch-up appearance

features.name: Large Meetings
features.description: Support for up to 1,000 video participants (Pro) and 10,000 view-only participants (Enterprise) with gallery, speaker, and immersive view layouts

features.name: Breakout Rooms
features.description: Split meeting participants into separate smaller groups with independent audio and video, timed sessions, and broadcast announcements

features.name: Team Chat
features.description: Persistent team messaging with channels, direct messages, file sharing, and message threading integrated with meeting scheduling

features.name: Zoom Phone
features.description: Cloud phone system with local numbers in 70+ countries, call routing, auto attendant, voicemail transcription, and SMS

features.name: Webinars
features.description: Large-scale broadcast meetings with registration pages, attendee reporting, Q&A moderation, polling, and panelist management

features.name: Zoom Events
features.description: Multi-session virtual event platform with ticketing, exhibitor booths, networking lounges, and on-demand replay

features.name: Meeting Recording
features.description: Cloud or local recording with auto-transcription, searchable transcripts, and shareable recording links

features.name: AI Companion
features.description: AI-generated meeting summaries, action item extraction, chat compose suggestions, and smart recording highlights

features.name: Zoom Rooms
features.description: Conference room software with calendar integration, wireless screen sharing, room booking, and digital signage

features.name: Closed Captioning
features.description: Real-time captions generated by AI or human captioners, with language translation support for multilingual meetings

features.name: Polls & Quizzes
features.description: In-meeting polling with multiple question types, quiz mode for training sessions, and results reporting

features.name: Whiteboard
features.description: Persistent collaborative whiteboard with sticky notes, shapes, drawing tools, and template library accessible before, during, and after meetings

features.name: End-to-End Encryption
features.description: 256-bit AES-GCM end-to-end encryption for meetings with up to 200 participants, enabled via toggle at meeting creation

features.name: App Integrations
features.description: Zoom App Marketplace with 2,000+ integrations including Slack, Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Salesforce, and HubSpot

features.name: Contact Center
features.description: Omnichannel contact center platform with voice, chat, email, social messaging, and AI-powered agent assistance

features.name: Scheduling and Calendar
features.description: Outlook, Google Calendar, and iCal integration with one-click meeting scheduling, calendar status, and alternative time suggestions

features.name: Analytics & Reports
features.description: Dashboard showing meeting usage, participant counts, duration trends, adoption metrics, and room utilization

content.title: Who Zoom Fits Best
content.body: Zoom is worth evaluating when an organization needs dependable video meetings, screen sharing, webinars, or room-based collaboration. It can suit external meetings where guests need a simple joining experience, as well as teams that use a broader set of Zoom communication products. Fit depends on meeting size, calendar and identity systems, recording rules, accessibility, and the organization's security requirements. Define the workflows that matter before comparing it with Webex, Microsoft Teams, or Google Meet.

content.title: Meetings and Guest Experience
content.body: Test the full meeting journey from scheduling to joining, sharing a screen, managing participants, and ending the session. Include external guests, mobile participants, low-bandwidth connections, captions, and users who need keyboard or accessibility support. Check how hosts control waiting rooms, participant permissions, chat, and screen sharing. A meeting platform should make the expected behavior easy to understand and should give hosts clear controls when an unexpected participant or disruption occurs.

content.title: Recording, Webinars, and Collaboration
content.body: If the organization uses recordings, webinars, rooms, or phone services, evaluate those workflows separately rather than assuming the core meeting plan includes them. Confirm where recordings are stored, who can access them, how long they are retained, and how they are shared or deleted. Test registration, moderation, and follow-up for events if relevant. Verify plan and licensing requirements for each capability in current official documentation.

content.title: Security and Administration
content.body: Review authentication, meeting access controls, encryption options, audit history, data retention, recording permissions, and administrative policy settings. Decide whether the organization needs single sign-on, managed devices, room controls, or region-specific data handling. Confirm how incidents are reported and how administrators can investigate unwanted access. Security and compliance claims should be checked against current vendor documentation and the exact service configuration; do not assume a certification or control applies to every plan.

content.title: Integrations and Operational Fit
content.body: Map the calendar, identity, chat, phone, learning, customer support, and room systems that Zoom must connect with. Test scheduling, joining links, user provisioning, and any workflow that moves information between systems. Document who owns each integration and how failures are reported. If the organization already uses Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace, test the end-to-end workflow in that environment rather than evaluating integrations from a feature list alone.

content.title: Limitations and Alternatives
content.body: Zoom may be less compelling if the organization wants every collaboration workflow centered in another suite or has strict requirements that its chosen plan cannot meet. Some capabilities require separate products, add-ons, or administrative setup. Compare the full workflow with Webex, Teams, and Meet: how guests join, how identity is managed, how meetings are recorded, and how support is handled. The best choice depends on the environment and requirements, not a universal claim about video quality.

content.title: Pricing and Plan Verification
content.body: Check Zoom's current official pricing for meeting limits, participant capacity, recording storage, webinar features, phone services, administration, support, and any required add-ons. Plan names and bundles can change. Compare the full cost for hosts, rooms, events, storage, and integrations, and include the effort required to configure and govern the service. Avoid relying on old starting prices or assuming a feature shown in a product overview is included in the selected plan.

content.title: Practical Recommendation
content.body: Pilot Zoom with the meetings and events the organization actually runs. Test guest joining, accessibility, host controls, recording permissions, integrations, and the support process. Agree on acceptance criteria before rollout and compare the results with the existing platform. Choose Zoom when its meeting experience and broader services fit the workflow; choose another option when suite integration, specific administrative controls, or regional requirements are more important.

faqs.question: Who should consider Zoom?
faqs.answer: Organizations that need video meetings, screen sharing, webinars, or room-based collaboration should test it against their meeting patterns, security requirements, and existing suite.

faqs.question: Does Zoom include webinars and phone services?
faqs.answer: Availability and licensing depend on the product and plan. Check current official documentation for each capability your organization needs.

faqs.question: What should we review for security?
faqs.answer: Check authentication, meeting access controls, recording permissions, retention, audit logs, and the current vendor documentation for the specific service and plan.

faqs.question: How much does Zoom cost?
faqs.answer: Pricing and bundles can change. Use the official pricing page and calculate the full cost for hosts, rooms, recordings, events, support, and add-ons.

faqs.question: How should we compare Zoom with Webex?
faqs.answer: Run the same meeting scenarios on both platforms and compare guest joining, host controls, accessibility, administration, integrations, recording policy, and total cost.

author: PilotStack Editorial Team
learningCurve: Minimal — most users can get started within an hour
whoShouldUse: Zoom is designed for fast-growing startups that need a scalable communication platform. Its generous free tier and flexible pricing make it accessible for early-stage companies.
whoShouldNotUse: Zoom may not be suitable for large enterprises with complex compliance requirements or teams needing extensive customization options. Organizations with more than 500 users may find the pricing less competitive at scale.
